One bar per day, running from your first unlock to your last screen. It is not how much you used the phone, it is how much of the day the phone was part of.

Your weekend looks like your Tuesday. 278 min at weekends against 255 on weekdays, and you are on the phone from 08:00 to midnight all seven days. You pick it up 17 times an hour and stay about 6.7 minutes each time — you are checking the phone, not sitting down with it (1.8 times more than A's rate of usage).

The daytime looks ordinary enough. But what happens when we turn the lights off?

Screen minutes between 23:00 and 06:00, night by night, for both people. This is the single chart the whole month turns on.

You are losing sleep. You started the month going to bed at 23:21 and ended it averaging 01:06, whilst always waking up at the same time — 08:43 then 08:54. You went from hardly unlocking your phone after midnight to doing it nearly 9 times a night. That is 95 minutes less rest, every night.

The same day-length bars, with the 23:00 to 06:00 band marked. What you are looking for is bars leaking into the band.

Unlocks after midnight, both people on the same scale. One of these two lines stays on the floor for thirty days.

The night-time usage increase is the main reason your wellbeing score has dropped so much. Sleep! It is the smallest number on this page — 30 min a day against 262 of screen — and it carries 20 % of the index, because an hour at 01:00 comes out of your rest and an hour at 17:00 does not.

Now you know when. The next question is what.

Your ten biggest apps by minutes. Colour is the content category; hover for how many times you opened each one.

The same, for websites. Only the domain is ever recorded, never the page — so time spent in the browser lands here rather than under Chrome.

What your minutes were made of, day by day, stacked. The order of the bands is fixed, so a band that grows really is growing and has not just been re-ranked.

You used 21 apps this month, with Spotify, WhatsApp and Messages holding 50 % of your usage — against A's 7 apps. You spent 2,186 min reaching people across 5 apps. Your distraction share is 17 %, barely above A's 15 %. What you spend your time on is completely ordinary. How much of it, and when, is not.

This chart only shows what actually opened, which is why Netflix and YouTube are barely on it: the filter stopped them 83 and 80 times and let through 3 and 4.

So why are they here at all? Were they downloaded that day? No. They were on the phone all month, and the filter blocked them on every one of the 30 days, a median of 14 times a day. Every minute they ever got comes from a single window on 18 May, when the filter stopped firing for about 22 hours. It came back the next morning and they were never opened again.

How is distraction measured? Not by how many apps you open. It is the share of your attributed time that landed in social, entertainment or gaming. Thirty apps for two minutes each is not distraction by this definition; one hour of one app is.

That is what got through. Here is what did not.

964 ordinary attempts, 194 to 339 a week, plus 121 adult and 82 gambling and 43 detections. None opened. The sensitive ones spike rather than trend: 145 of 203 land in weeks 2 and 3 and 30 in week 4. That is a summary entry, not a phone call.

This screen stays on the device. The weekly summary carries the filter's state and that 203 sensitive attempts were blocked and none opened. Nothing named.

The phone knew all of this. Here is what it decided to say about it, and what it kept to itself.
